title: Efficient Circuit Transpilation of Commuting Gates on 2D Grids
abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are central to many applications but can be challenging to solve. Quantum approaches such as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) offer new tools with which to tackle such problems. However, QAOA circuits inherit the interaction structure of the target Hamiltonian, often resulting in deep circuits when compiled onto hardware with limited connectivity. Efficient transpilation is therefore critical to their practical performance. In this work, we propose a transpilation scheme for circuits consisting of blocks of commuting two-qubit gates on two-dimensional lattices. Unlike standard approaches based on random initial mappings and fixed routing, our method alternates between constructing problem-dependent SWAP-layer sequences and updating the qubit layout. By adapting the routing to the required interactions, this yields significantly shorter circuits for graphs with few edges. We benchmark our approach on QAOA instances for Maximum Cut (MC) on Random Regular graphs and Maximum Independent Set (MIS) on Erdős-Rényi graphs. Compared to standard methods, we reduce circuit depth and gate count by about a factor of two, enabling experiments with up to $80$ qubits and improving approximation ratios by up to $6.6\%$ for MC and $9.3\%$ for MIS.
summary: This paper presents a novel transpilation scheme for mapping quantum circuits involving commuting gates onto 2D lattice hardware. By iteratively optimizing both the required SWAP layers and the qubit layout, it achieves substantial reductions in circuit depth compared to existing methods. This efficiency boost allows for testing larger-scale QAOA applications on hard combinatorial problems.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing efficient transpilation schemes for quantum circuits, particularly those involving blocks of commuting two-qubit gates, to run on hardware with limited connectivity.
main_result: The proposed greedy transpilation scheme significantly reduces circuit depth and gate count (by a factor of two) compared to standard methods, enabling larger qubit counts and improving approximation ratios for optimization problems like Max Cut and MIS.
method: The authors propose an iterative method that alternates between constructing problem-dependent SWAP-layer sequences and optimizing the initial qubit layout by adapting routing directly to required interactions.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum computation implemented on a two-dimensional lattice grid. The circuits are used for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to combinatorial optimization problems like Maximum Cut (MC) and Maximum Independent Set (MIS).
key_observables: Circuit depth, gate count, mean approximation ratio, and kept shot ratio.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n$), the circuit depth parameter ($p$) in QAOA, and the graph structure (Random Regular or Erdős-Rényi graphs).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the underlying hardware supports two-dimensional grid connectivity; standard optimal qubit routing is noted to be NP-complete.
figures_summary: Figures compare circuit complexity (SWAP layers, CZ gates) across various transpilation strategies (linear, hybrid, greedy) on different graph types. Other figures illustrate the search process and performance metrics like approximation ratios vs. qubits.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of efficient transpilation for QAOA circuits on 2D grids. It details the proposed greedy strategy by optimizing both SWAP layer sequences and initial mappings, benchmarking it against established line-based and grid-based reference strategies across MC and MIS instances.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization algorithms, the underlying need to map abstract Hamiltonians onto physical hardware connectivity maps directly to resource constraints in simulating complex quantum many-body systems or designing quantum network protocols.

Figure 2: Linear and hybrid strategy on a 4 × 4 rectan- gular grid coupling map. Both strategies route along the longest line of qubits (red), but the hybrid strategy can additionally apply interactions on the remaining edges of the coupling map (light blue).

Figure 3: Greedy searches a tree of SWAP layer se- quences. The edges correspond to SWAP layers and are colored according to the basis Bgrid shown in Fig. 1. The nodes encode qubit layouts π and the remaining inter- actions Erem. At depth k = 1, possible layouts are de- noted by π01, π02, π03, π04, corresponding to their respect- ive SWAP sequences. The tree is explored up to a fixed depth kmax, after which a leaf minimizing the number of remaining edges is selected to continue the search until all interactions are implemented, yielding Sgreedy.
